summary: For children aged 7–9: build the habit of asking 'what ELSE could explain this?' after any result. The teaching objective is for a child to generate two or more plausible alternative explanations for the same observation and recognise that MORE evidence is needed to decide between them, rather than locking onto the first idea that fits. The central worked example is a wilted houseplant with several rival causes (too little water, too much water, no light, too cold, bugs), where incoming clues support some explanations and rule out others.
misconceptions: Assuming the first explanation that fits must be the correct one.
Thinking there is only ever one possible explanation for a result.
Believing a single clue settles the matter, without checking it against rival explanations.
Generating alternatives but then not seeing that more evidence is needed to choose.
Defending a favourite explanation instead of weighing it fairly against others.
Treating 'I'm not sure which yet' as failure rather than honest, in-progress science.

activities.title: Explanation Detective Board: one clue is rarely enough
steps: Look at a result on the board — a houseplant has wilted — and, instead of guessing THE reason, propose or select as many plausible 'suspects' as you can: TOO LITTLE WATER, TOO MUCH WATER, NO LIGHT, TOO COLD, BUGS.
Earn credit for each additional plausible explanation you add, so proposing a second and third idea is the scored move, not just picking one.

Reveal clues one at a time and mark how each clue affects every suspect: for 'the soil is soggy and wet', strike through TOO LITTLE WATER and brighten TOO MUCH WATER; for 'the identical plant next to it in the same dark corner is thriving', strike through NO LIGHT and also TOO COLD, because both plants share the same spot, so they get the same light and the same warmth.
Watch the field of surviving explanations narrow with each clue, and notice when a confident first guess (it looked dry, so — no water!) gets eliminated by the soggy-soil clue.
When two suspects are still standing, answer the closing prompt: 'what one clue would tell them apart?' — pairing each surviving explanation with the evidence that would distinguish it.
activities.insight: The first explanation that fits a result is not automatically the right one; usually more than one idea can account for the same observation, so you deliberately hold several open and gather more evidence to decide between them.

activities.title: Detective dialogue: 'good — what else?'
steps: Talk through a result with an in-role investigator who, each time you give one explanation, asks 'good — what ELSE could explain that?' and refuses to let you settle on the first idea.
For each pair of rival explanations, say what evidence would tell them apart ('what would tell us which is right?').
Practise saying 'I'm not sure yet' as a legitimate scientific position while you gather more evidence.
activities.insight: Asking for another explanation, and for the evidence that would decide between explanations, is a repeatable reasoning habit you can apply to any result.

activities.title: Primer: one result, several possible causes
steps: Explore a mystery scene where tapping each hotspot reveals a different possible explanation for the same result, so you see several explanations can fit one observation.
Use this as a warm-up before the detective board, then move on to generating your own alternatives.
activities.insight: A single result can have several possible causes — more than one idea can fit what you observed.

activities.title: Check: name another explanation and the test that decides
steps: Read a short scenario: a plant on the windowsill grew tall and one in the cupboard stayed short; a friend says 'the windowsill plant grew because someone talked to it every morning.'
List as many other explanations as you can for why the windowsill plant grew taller (e.g. more light, more warmth, more water).

For a chosen pair of explanations, say how you would find out which one is really right — for example, growing two matching plants in the cupboard with the same water and warmth, talking to only one of them every morning, and comparing their growth to see whether talking alone makes a difference.

Answer recognition items such as 'which of these is ALSO a possible explanation?' and 'what evidence would help decide between these two?', framed as 'the first idea was X; what else could explain the result?'
activities.insight: Strong reasoning produces more than one plausible explanation rather than accepting the first, and treats rivals as competing candidates that must be tested against each other.

checkQuestion: A plant on the windowsill grew tall and one in the cupboard stayed short. Your friend says 'the windowsill plant grew because someone talked to it every morning.' Could there be another explanation for why it grew taller? Tell me as many as you can.
checkAnswer: Strong reasoning generates more than one plausible explanation rather than accepting the first — most obviously that the windowsill plant got light (or warmth, or water) the cupboard plant didn't — and recognises that the talking explanation is only one of several possibilities that would need to be tested against each other. The mark of it is actively producing alternatives, not defending or settling on one.
